## Muscles, Scapulae, Wrists, and Biological Ambiguity {#sec-lay-ch25}

## A Concrete Picture

Several teams can move the same piano through a doorway. One pushes, another
pulls with straps, and a third combines both. The piano can follow the same path
while the people share the load differently. Watching the piano does not reveal
each person's force or establish equal effort.

Club motion poses a similar inverse problem. A net grip wrench describes the
combined force and moment acting on the club. It does not usually identify the
separate hand loads, anatomical joint moments, muscle forces, or neural commands
behind that result. These are successive inference problems with different
unknowns. Resolving one does not automatically resolve the next.

![Different Feasible Biological Allocations Can Share a Resultant Grip Wrench.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_biological_redundancy.svg){#fig-lay-biological-redundancy width=98% fig-alt="Conceptual diagram connecting scapula, shoulder, elbow, forearm, and wrist contributions to a resultant grip wrench. Internal load, stiffness, and effort may differ between feasible allocations. The arrows are not independent actuators or measured pathways."}

The anatomical boxes are coupled parts of a body, not five interchangeable
actuators. Different allocations must still satisfy anatomy, contact
constraints, force limits, and state history.

## How the Mechanism Works

### Three Different Inverse Problems

First, a rigid-club model can infer a resultant grip wrench from motion and
inertia, after accounting for gravity and other external loads. Second, body
inverse dynamics can estimate net joint moments if segment motion, inertial
parameters, and the necessary external loads are known. A net club wrench alone
generally leaves the separate hand loads underdetermined in the two-arm closed
chain. Third, a musculoskeletal model allocates joint demand among muscles and
passive tissues.

### Two Allocations With the Same Full Club Wrench

Separate contact ambiguity from muscle ambiguity. Fix a club reference $O$ and
contact points $\mathbf r_L=(-0.1,0,0)$ and
$\mathbf r_R=(0.1,0,0)\,\mathrm m$. All components below use one right-handed
frame. Here $\mathbf F_i$ is hand $i$'s force and $\mathbf C_i$ is its
contact couple; both act **on the club**:

| Allocation | $F_{Ly}$ (N) | $F_{Ry}$ (N) | $C_{Lz}$ (N m) | $C_{Rz}$ (N m) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | -10 | 110 | 0 | 0 |
| B | 30 | 70 | 4 | 4 |

All unlisted components vanish. Both allocations satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F&=\mathbf F_L+\mathbf F_R=(0,100,0)\,\mathrm N,\\
\mathbf M_O&=\sum_{i=L,R}(\mathbf r_i\times\mathbf F_i+\mathbf C_i)
=(0,0,12)\,\mathrm{N\,m}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-lay-biology-matched-wrench}

A obtains all $12\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ from the force distribution. B obtains
$4\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ that way and $8\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ from contact moments.
These are full resultant-wrench matches within an ideal contact model.
Grip pressure, friction, and tissue limits determine actual feasibility.

The equal force at each hand, $\mathbf F_c=\mathbf F/2$, contributes
$(\mathbf r_L+\mathbf r_R)\times\mathbf F_c=0$ at this midpoint. Changing arm
posture while keeping the contact points, force components, and reference fixed
cannot create a new common-force moment arm. Physically shifting both contacts
$0.02\,\mathrm m$ along $+x$ relative to the same $O$ raises the moment to
$14\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ if the loads are retained. That is changed geometry and a
changed wrench, not a third allocation matching the original task. Changing
only the reporting origin is a separate wrench-transport operation.

At the same rigid-club twist, $\mathbf v_O=(0,2,0)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and
$\boldsymbol\omega=(0,0,3)\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, both allocations deliver
$\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v_O+\mathbf M_O\cdot\boldsymbol\omega=236\,\mathrm W$.
Summing contact powers with
$\mathbf v_i=\mathbf v_O+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_i$
gives the same answer: left/right contributions are $-17/253\,\mathrm W$
for A and $63/173\,\mathrm W$ for B. Equal total club power does not identify each
hand's contribution or each muscle's expenditure. Bilateral wrench sensing
addresses the first ambiguity; anatomical and physiological evidence addresses
the second.

### Matching a Scalar Task Is Weaker Than Matching a Wrench

The companion benchmark in UpstreamDrift, linked below at its reviewed revision,
matches a same-state control-induced angular-acceleration target expressed in
moment units: $I_C\ddot\alpha_{C,u}=8\,\mathrm{N\,m}$. Here $I_C$ is the
model club's planar rotational inertia, and
$\ddot\alpha_{C,u}$ is the control-induced part of its angular acceleration. It subtracts the zero-control
acceleration at the same state and allocates controls within proximal and wrist
generalized-torque subspaces. This scalar constraint does not by itself match
all resultant-force components, the full grip wrench, or a future trajectory.
The table above demonstrates a different, explicitly full-wrench construction.

For a rigid club with identical initial state and other external loads,
identical resultant-wrench histories expressed consistently imply identical
rigid-club motion. Matching one instantaneous moment, one speed, or one scalar
acceleration does not supply those conditions. Shaft deformation adds states if
the club is not modeled as rigid. Name precisely which task was held equal
before interpreting a successful simulation.

### From Joint Demand to Muscle Forces

Let $\boldsymbol\tau_{\mathrm{ID}}$ denote the joint demand remaining after
the chosen inverse-dynamics formulation accounts for external loads and
constraint reactions. One declared allocation model is

$$
\boldsymbol\tau_{\mathrm{ID}}
=R(q)\mathbf F_{\mathrm{mt}}+\boldsymbol\tau_{\mathrm{passive}},
\qquad
R_{ji}=-\frac{\partial\ell_i}{\partial q_j}.
$$ {#eq-lay-biology-allocation}

Here $q$ collects joint coordinates, $\mathbf F_{\mathrm{mt}}$ collects
musculotendon tensions, $\ell_i$ is musculotendon path length, $F_i\geq0$ is its tensile force,
and $R_{ji}$ is its signed moment arm about rotational coordinate $q_j$.
A positive entry means tension produces positive generalized torque. Separate
passive joint loads exclude passive muscle contributions already included in
$F_i$. Grip forces and joint reactions must not be added again if the
inverse-dynamics demand already accounts for them.

More muscles than independent joint equations permits a force-map null space,
but does not guarantee an unlimited feasible family. Nonnegative tension,
strength limits, tendon state, activation history, and measurements constrain
it. An allocation can be infeasible, unique, or nonunique. Optimization selects
a solution conditional on its cost and constraints; it does not identify a
neural strategy merely by producing a smooth answer [@zajac1989].

### A Bounded Muscle Example

Consider a manufactured one-joint example with opposing moment arms of
$+0.03$ and $-0.03\,\mathrm m$, zero separate passive torque, and a required
moment of $3\,\mathrm{N\,m}$. Suppose $0\leq F_A\leq300\,\mathrm N$ and
$0\leq F_B\leq200\,\mathrm N$. In SI units,

$$
0.03(F_A-F_B)=3,\qquad
F_A=F_B+100,\qquad 0\leq F_B\leq200.
$$ {#eq-lay-biology-bounded-forces}

The pairs $(100,0)$, $(200,100)$, and $(300,200)\,\mathrm N$ produce the same
net moment with different individual forces. Pairs outside the bounds are
inadmissible. Pairs inside them are only instantaneously feasible; generating
their histories also requires compatible muscle and tendon dynamics.
Specifying those internal states can remove ambiguity that remains when only
net torque is known.

At $\dot q=2\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, the two path-length rates are
$-0.06$ and $+0.06\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Every listed pair gives

$$
P_{\mathrm{paths}}=-\sum_iF_i\dot\ell_i
=\tau_{\mathrm{muscle}}\dot q=6\,\mathrm W.
$$ {#eq-lay-biology-path-power}

Here $\tau_{\mathrm{muscle}}=\sum_i r_i F_i$ is the net torque from the
musculotendon paths, including any passive force they contain.
This virtual-work equality gives net musculotendon power delivered to the
modeled coordinate, not each muscle fibre's power or metabolic expenditure.
Tendon storage and pennation separate fibre mechanics from path mechanics.
Equal net joint power does not make the allocations biologically
interchangeable. These numbers illustrate accounting, not fitted golfer
parameters.

### Electrical Excitation, Activation, and Force

Surface EMG measures electrical potentials associated with muscle-fibre action
potentials in an electrode's detection region. With suitable processing it
informs sampled excitation, not a direct force or activation-state measurement.
Activation dynamics link excitation to contractile state; contraction mechanics
depend on length, velocity, history, architecture, and tendon loading.
Normalization does not remove those dependencies. Electrode position, tissue
conduction, cancellation, and cross-talk also limit comparisons
[@vigotsky2018EMG].

A detected burst alone establishes neither joint-torque magnitude nor the sign
of club power. An apparently silent channel cannot exclude force: passive
tension, retained internal state, unmeasured muscles, and detection limits
remain possibilities. EMG helps discriminate candidate timings and constrain
models when its measurement assumptions are explicit. It does not replace the
mechanical measurements needed to test a proposed force or power pathway.

### Co-Contraction, Stiffness, and Impedance

Opposing muscle forces can increase without changing net torque. Whether this
improves resistance to disturbance requires a different measurement: the
response to a perturbation about a declared state. Stiffness, damping, inertia,
and delayed feedback contribute differently to mechanical impedance. A
moment-versus-angle slope traced during a swing also contains changes in
activation and history; it is not automatically the local stiffness measured
by perturbing a specified state.

For a one-coordinate elastic illustration, hold activation and other internal
variables fixed, set $k_i=\partial F_i/\partial\ell_i$, and use
$r_i=-\partial\ell_i/\partial q$. The restoring stiffness contribution is

$$
K=-\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial q}
=\sum_i\left(k_i r_i^2-F_i\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial q}\right).
$$ {#eq-lay-biology-geometric-stiffness}

The first term maps material stiffness through the moment arm. The second
comes from changing geometry. At fixed moment arms, larger positive local
muscle stiffness increases the first term. Geometry, other tissues, and
feedback prevent that observation from becoming a universal claim about
whole-joint or whole-swing stability. Joint compression likewise requires force
directions and joint equilibrium, not just a scalar net moment.

A manufactured counterexample makes the geometric term visible. Near $q=0$,
use path changes $\Delta\ell_1=-0.03q-0.01q^2$ and
$\Delta\ell_2=0.03q$ in metres, with $F_i=100+1000\Delta\ell_i$ in newtons.
Here radians are dimensionless, and the coefficients carry the corresponding
SI units. Both tensile paths have positive $1000\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$
stiffness. At zero angle their net torque is zero, but the restoring stiffness
is $1.8-2.0=-0.2\,\mathrm{N\,m\,rad^{-1}}$. Holding the moment arms constant
instead gives $+1.8\,\mathrm{N\,m\,rad^{-1}}$. Positive element stiffness alone
does not determine generalized restoring stiffness. This is a counterexample
for two ideal elastic paths, not a stability assessment of a human joint.

Hu, Murray, and Perreault combined a short-range-stiffness model with an
upper-limb model and compared it with previously collected small-perturbation
endpoint-stiffness measurements from five people. Their formulation includes
moment-arm geometry; the tested conditions involved specified postures and
voluntary forces. It supports studying this mechanism, not a claim that rapid
golf transition dynamics or an optimal co-contraction strategy has been
validated [@hu2011ShortRange].

### Tendons Store Energy

An elastic tendon stores strain energy, not force. For an ideal linear element
$F=kx$, with extension $x$ from its unloaded reference,

$$
\Delta E=\int_{x_0}^{x_1}F(x)\,dx
=\tfrac12 k(x_1^2-x_0^2).
$$ {#eq-lay-biology-tendon-energy}

With $k=10{,}000\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, extension from $5$ to $10\,\mathrm{mm}$
raises force from $50$ to $100\,\mathrm N$ and stores an additional
$0.375\,\mathrm J$. Force is an instantaneous load; stored energy accounts for
work. A static force-extension law contains no time delay. Force-rise timing
requires system dynamics, including excitation, contraction, movement, and any
dissipative behavior. Compliance can affect that timing but is not itself a
fixed delay.

For two positive linear stiffnesses in series,
$k_{\mathrm{eq}}^{-1}=k_1^{-1}+k_2^{-1}$; a compliant tendon can limit the
effective stiffness of the combined path. Tendon slack length in a model defines
a force-length reference. It is not evidence for a backlash-like interval at a
golfer's wrist.

The UpstreamDrift benchmark also studies a separate synthetic law: a rotational dead zone,
linear transmitted torque beyond it, and first-order deflection dynamics.
Its persistent-direction advantage disappears in its declared zero-dead-zone
comparison. That result is conditional on the chosen transmission family.
Neither the calculation nor a sensation of firmness establishes a human
transmission gap. Muscle short-range stiffness, tendon elasticity, grip contact,
and shaft deformation need distinct state descriptions and tests.

### Scapula, Forearm, and Wrist Are Distinct Parts

Scapulothoracic motion describes the scapula moving relative to the thorax; it
is not a fixed hinge. Scapular orientation changes the orientation of the glenoid
and the geometry available to the arm. Distinguish clavicle, scapula, and humerus
when reporting shoulder motion. The International Society of Biomechanics (ISB) recommendations provide a
reporting framework, not a shortcut from one reduced shoulder torque to an
identified scapular action
([Wu et al., 2005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbiomech.2004.05.042)).

Forearm pronation and supination involve the radioulnar mechanism; they are
distinct from wrist flexion-extension and radial-ulnar deviation. They interact
in orienting a gripping hand. A planar model's wrist coordinate represents its
declared relative rotation. Projecting a three-dimensional moment onto an axis
gives an axis moment, but it is a work-conjugate generalized torque only when
the coordinate-to-angular-velocity mapping justifies it.

A grip contact moment is not automatically an anatomical wrist joint moment.
Segment inertia, forces, lever arms, and muscle loads intervene. An opposing
club-moment contribution can coexist with positive translational contact power
or active muscles. Pair the correct wrench and velocity before classifying
power; an opposing moment alone does not identify a passive tissue mechanism.

Skin-mounted measurements need a validated relationship to bone motion.
Ludewig and colleagues used bone-fixed tracking to study shoulder-complex motion
during arm elevation in twelve people; this describes their measurement scope,
not a golf-specific scapular force pathway
([Ludewig et al., 2009](https://doi.org/10.2106/JBJS.G.01483)).
Testing a proposed scapular contribution to bilateral hand loads needs compatible
kinematics, load measurements, and an anatomical model with uncertainty.
Renaming an abstract arm driver cannot provide those observations.

### What the Golf EMG Studies Establish

Kao, Pink, Jobe, and Perry studied fifteen competitive male golfers with
bilateral EMG of four scapular muscles and cinematography [@kao1995].
Their phase-dependent observations concern those sampled muscles and
participants, not a uniquely identified two-hand wrench allocation.

Robinson and colleagues studied bilateral extensor carpi ulnaris activity and
wrist kinematics in fifteen subelite, right-handed men [@robinson2023].
This is one selected muscle on each side, not a complete wrist-muscle inventory.
The reported absence of a significant downswing EMG association with impact
clubhead kinematics does not establish equivalence or mechanical irrelevance.
Both studies motivate specific anatomical questions; neither resolves muscle
forces from club motion or proves the proposed preload benefit.

### A Biological Comparison That Can Fail

The working hypothesis remains worth testing: directionally persistent loading
might preserve useful force transmission for some golfers, while another
allocation might reduce effort or suit different anatomy. Neither mechanics
example chooses a universal strategy.

Select measurements for the hypothesis. To distinguish contact allocations,
measure bilateral wrenches at declared reference points and check resultant
closure. To investigate stiffness, define the perturbation or identified
dynamic model, amplitude, time window, and feedback assumptions. To test an
anatomical pathway, add suitable segment kinematics and muscle observations.
Ultrasound or other internal-state measurements may help particular tendon
questions; not every study requires every sensor. The linked protocol specifies
a particular combined test, not a universal minimum for biological claims.

Randomizing instructions can estimate the effect of assigned instructions under
a sound experimental design. It does not randomize the muscle allocation
actually adopted. Check whether the intended load pattern changed. Association
among a cue, stiffness, and outcome does not alone establish causal mediation;
confounding and other pathways remain. Prespecify contrasts, uncertainty,
alternative explanations, and participant-level holdout.

A failed wrench-closure check challenges the mechanical reconstruction.
A well-measured mismatch between predicted and observed scapular motion
challenges that anatomical mapping. Ambiguous EMG or unresolved alternatives
can leave the biological question inconclusive even when contact mechanics
remains supported. Separating these outcomes helps avoid attributing failures to an
unspecified hidden muscle strategy.

### Reader Lab: Follow the Evidence in Both Directions

Start with allocations A and B. Compute force, moment, and power, then identify
the bilateral measurements that distinguish them. Next hold a net joint moment
fixed and construct two candidates from the bounded antagonist example.
State which internal measurements or model assumptions could reject one.
Do not call a modeled joint reaction a directly measured force.

Reverse the exercise from an EMG burst. Identify the sampled region,
processing, normalization, and timing uncertainty. List the additional state
and mechanics needed to infer force, joint torque, and club power. A statement
of sampled excitation cannot skip those steps. Contact mechanics and biology
inform one another without becoming interchangeable.

## Where the Picture Breaks

Piano teams choose explicit roles. Human control also involves distributed
coordination, feedback, and history. Coaching words such as push, pull, firm,
and passive do not specify a muscle allocation or a state equation.

More anatomical detail adds parameters as well as explanatory possibilities.
Uncertain paths or tendon properties can dominate an optimized answer.
Report sensitivity and feasible alternatives instead of equating detail with
identification. Similar club speed does not establish similar internal loading
or safety; these examples do not evaluate clinical outcomes.

A useful biological claim states the observation, mechanical demand, anatomical
mapping, alternatives, and uncertainty. It may show consistency with evidence,
contradict a pathway, or identify a discriminating measurement. Ambiguity becomes
productive when it specifies the next test.
